hook: Your advice was good. So why did they get more upset?
title: Three Kinds of Conversation

steps.scenario: Your friend says: 'My boss rewrote my whole report in front of everyone.' You reply…

options.text: Next time, send him a draft a day early.
options.feedback: Solid advice — for a practical talk. But this one sounds like it's about feelings first. Solutions land better after they feel heard.

options.text: In front of everyone? That sounds humiliating.
options.feedback: Yes. This is an emotional conversation. Naming the feeling tells them you're on the same channel.

options.text: My boss does that too, it's so annoying.
options.feedback: Friendly instinct, but it moves the spotlight to you. Stay on their story a bit longer.

steps.scenario: Later they say: 'OK, I'm calmer. What should I actually do on Monday?' Now you…

options.text: Keep validating: 'That must have felt awful.'
options.feedback: Kind, but they just switched channels. They're asking for a plan now.

options.text: Offer two concrete options and ask which fits.
options.feedback: Right. The talk turned practical, so you turned with it. Matching is a moving target.

options.text: Ask what this says about who they are at work.
options.feedback: That's a social/identity question. Could matter later — but they asked for a next step.

insight: Most talks are one of three kinds: practical (what should we do?), emotional (how do we feel?), or social (who are we?). Advice given in an emotional talk often misses. Notice which kind you're in — and when it switches.
model: Ask: is this about solving, feeling, or identity? Then answer in that same channel.
try_today: In your next real conversation, silently label it practical, emotional, or social before you reply.

hook: Want someone to calm down? Stop trying to convince them.
title: Looping for Understanding

steps.scenario: Your partner snaps: 'You never help with the dishes!' You actually did them twice this week. You say…

options.text: That's not true, I did them Tuesday and Thursday.
options.feedback: Accurate — and it will probably start a fact fight. They don't feel heard yet, so facts sound like defense.

options.text: It sounds like you feel you're carrying most of the housework. Is that right?
options.feedback: That's a loop: repeat the heart of it, then check. You can share your facts after they say 'yes, exactly.'

options.text: Let's not do this right now.
options.feedback: Taking a break can be wise. But without a loop first, it can feel like a door closing.

steps.scenario: They answer: 'Not exactly — it's that I always have to ask.' You…

options.text: Ah, so it's less the dishes and more having to be the one who notices. Right?
options.feedback: Perfect. A loop that gets corrected isn't a failure — it's the loop working. Now you know the real issue.

options.text: Well, you could just ask nicely.
options.feedback: Understandable reflex, but it skips past what they just told you. Loop once more.

insight: Looping means: ask, repeat back what you heard in your own words, then check if you got it right. People soften when they're proven heard — not just told 'I hear you.' Getting corrected is part of the method.
model: Ask → say it back in your words → 'Did I get that right?' → repeat until they say yes.
try_today: In one conversation today, say back what you heard and ask 'Did I get that right?' before giving your view.

hook: 'I hear you' is not proof. Can you build the real thing?
title: The Loop, Step by Step

game.prompt: Put the steps of looping for understanding in order
items: Say back the core of it in your own words
game.explain: The key is the check at the end. Summarizing without asking is still a guess. Asking turns your guess into shared understanding.

insight: Listening is invisible; looping makes it visible. The person hears their idea in your words and gets a chance to fix it. That moment of 'yes, that's it' is often when tension drops.
model: Understanding isn't what you feel — it's what the other person confirms.
try_today: Pick one person today and do one full loop, ending with 'Did I get that right?'

hook: After a great party, do you feel charged up or drained?
title: Where You Recharge

questions.q: After a long day of meetings, I want…

options.label: A quiet room and no talking

questions.q: When I have a hard problem, I…

options.label: Talk it out to figure it out

questions.q: A free Saturday with no plans feels…
In a loud, busy room I…

zones.label: Introvert-leaning
zones.text: You probably recharge best in quiet. That's not shyness — you can be warm and bold and still need solitude to refuel.

zones.label: Ambivert zone
zones.text: Like many people, you sit near the middle. Your need for people vs. quiet may shift with sleep, stress, and who's around.

zones.label: Extrovert-leaning
zones.text: You likely get energy from people and stimulation. Quiet focus may need a bit more structure for you to enjoy.

insight: Introversion isn't shyness; it's mostly about how much stimulation feels good. Most people land near the middle, not at the poles. 'Recharge' is a handy lens, but researchers still debate what extraversion really measures.
model: Not shy vs. loud — notice what drains you and what refuels you, then plan around it.
try_today: Look at tomorrow's schedule and add one 10-minute recharge block that fits your end of the spectrum.

hook: If every human vanished tonight, would your cash be worth a cent?
title: Shared Stories

game.prompt: Would it still exist if no human believed in it?

items.why: The paper stays. Its value lives in what millions of people agree to accept.
Rock doesn't need anyone's belief. The name 'Everest' does, though.
Rivers are real; the line on the map is an agreement people keep.
Harari's example: a company exists in law and shared belief, not in its buildings.
It pulls whether anyone believes or not.
The Earth's orbit is real; the meaning of the date is a story we share.

insight: Harari argues humans cooperate in huge numbers because we believe the same stories — money, laws, nations. 'Fiction' doesn't mean fake or bad: these stories are tools. The trick is remembering they can be rewritten.
model: Some things are rocks, some are agreements. Agreements can be questioned — and changed.
try_today: Name one 'rule' you follow today and ask: is this a rock or an agreement? Who could change it?

source.work: Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind (2011)

hook: Can you argue the other side so well they'd thank you?
title: Steelmanning

steps.scenario: Your friend thinks phones should be banned in schools. You disagree. Which reply is a steelman?

options.text: So you think teens are too dumb to handle a phone?
options.feedback: That's a strawman — a weaker version that's easy to knock down. They'd likely just get annoyed.

options.text: You're worried phones pull kids' attention away from learning and from each other, and a clear rule is easier than constant fights. Fair?
options.feedback: Steelman. It's their best version, in words they'd agree with. Now your disagreement will actually be heard.

options.text: Whatever, people said the same about TV.
options.feedback: Might be a real point later, but it skips their argument instead of meeting it.

options.text: Say where you agree, then share your concern about emergencies and teaching phone skills.
options.feedback: Great. Agreement first, then disagreement. This is close to Rapoport's rules as Dennett describes them.
You earned the floor, so don't spend it on 'you're wrong.' Start with what you share.

insight: A strawman attacks the weakest version of a view. A steelman restates the strongest one first. It makes you fairer, makes others listen, and sometimes shows you that you were the one missing something.
model: Before you disagree, state their view so well they say 'yes, exactly.'
try_today: Pick a view you disagree with and write its strongest case in 3 sentences — as if you believed it.

source.work: Intuition Pumps and Other Tools for Thinking (2013)

hook: Fair criticism has 4 steps. Most of us jump straight to step 4.
title: Rapoport's Rules

game.prompt: Order the steps for criticizing someone's view fairly
items: Restate their view so clearly they wish they'd said it that way
List the points where you agree
Mention anything you learned from them
game.explain: Daniel Dennett popularized these as 'Rapoport's Rules,' crediting the game theorist Anatol Rapoport. By step 4, the other person is far more ready to listen.

insight: Criticism lands better after the other person feels understood and respected. These rules slow you down just enough to check you're arguing with their real view — not one you invented.
model: Restate → agree → learn → then critique. Earn the right to disagree.
try_today: Next time you disagree in a chat or meeting, do steps 1 and 2 out loud before your point.

source.work: Intuition Pumps and Other Tools for Thinking (2013)

hook: You think people will say no if you ask for help. Want the real odds?
title: Asking for Help Is Brave

game.prompt: In a study, people had to ask strangers to fill out a short form. To get 5 yeses, how many did they guess they'd need to ask?
choices: About as many as it took
About twice as many as it took
game.reveal: They guessed about twice as many as it took. Strangers were far more willing to help than askers expected (Flynn & Lake, 2008); later studies by Vanessa Bohns found the same.

insight: We tend to underestimate how often others will say yes — partly because we focus on the cost of helping, while they feel the awkwardness of saying no. Asking isn't weakness; it's often what lets connection start.
model: Others say yes more than you predict. 'Help' is a short, brave word.
try_today: Ask one person for a small, specific bit of help today — and notice how they actually respond.

source.work: Flynn & Lake, 'If You Need Help, Just Ask' (2008); The Boy, the Mole, the Fox and the Horse (2019)
